back: The amount of substance containing $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles (the Avogadro constant).
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol⁻¹ — numerically equal to its relative formula mass.

front: Link amount, mass and molar mass.
back: $n = \dfrac{m}{M}$
$c = \dfrac{n}{V}$, with $V$ in dm³; $c$ in mol dm⁻³.
Empirical: simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. Molecular: actual number of each atom in a molecule — a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

front: How do you convert cm³ to dm³?
back: Divide by 1000 (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³).

front: Relative formula mass vs molar mass?
back: Mr: sum of Ar values, no units. M: same number, units g mol⁻¹.
Equal volumes of gases at the same T and p contain equal numbers of molecules — volume ratio = mole ratio.
$c_1V_1 = c_2V_2$ (amount of solute unchanged).

front: Linking number of particles and amount?
back: $N = n \times N_A$, with $N_A = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ mol⁻¹.

front: How many atoms are in 1 mol of H₂O?
back: 3 mol of atoms ($3 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}$) — one mole of molecules contains 3 moles of atoms. State which particle you are counting.
Assume 100 g → mass of each element ÷ Ar → divide by smallest → multiply to whole numbers if needed (e.g. 1.5 → ×2).
Multiplier = M ÷ M(empirical formula); multiply every subscript. E.g. CH₂O with M = 180 g mol⁻¹ → C₆H₁₂O₆.
All C → CO₂ (n(C) = n(CO₂)); all H → H₂O (n(H) = 2n(H₂O)); O by difference in mass; then find the ratio.
Mass concentration in g dm⁻³; molar concentration in mol dm⁻³. Convert: g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M.
The concentration of HCl in mol dm⁻³. 1 mol dm⁻³ is also written 1 M (molar).
Mass of solute per 10⁶ units of mass of solution (≈ mg per kg, or mg dm⁻³ for dilute aqueous solutions); used for very low concentrations.

front: Volume of O₂ needed to burn 10 cm³ of CH₄ (same T, p)?
back: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; volume ratio = mole ratio, so 20 cm³ of O₂.

front: SI unit and symbol for amount of substance?
back: Mole, symbol mol; quantity symbol n.

front: Percentage by mass of an element in a compound?
back: % = (number of atoms × Ar) ÷ Mr × 100. E.g. N in NH₄NO₃: 28/80 × 100 = 35%.
Heat to constant mass; n(H₂O lost) = mass lost/18.02; n(CuSO₄) = mass of residue/159.6; x = ratio.
